description: I'm a Computer Science Engineering student and full-stack developer passionate about technology, innovation, and problem-solving. I enjoy building web applications, designing intuitive user interfaces, and turning creative ideas into practical solutions. As a member of SkyRift, I'm excited to collaborate, explore new technologies, and contribute to an innovative space mission design experience for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Project Summary
SKY RIFT: Orbital Frontier is a browser game that teaches the trade-offs of real space mission design. Players pick a mission (Earth orbit, Moon, Mars or asteroid Bennu), build a spacecraft in a 3D hangar, choose a rocket, pass a preflight check, then fly the mission turn by turn.
Every choice has a visible consequence. Adding an instrument changes mass, power, fuel and cost. Preflight explains each blocker in plain language, such as "Δv short by 233 m/s". In flight, players observe, downlink data or conserve power while anomalies like solar storms and ground-station dropouts force decisions. A debrief explains why the mission succeeded or failed and what to change.
Learning stays in context: short hints, "What real missions do" notes, a Learn page on the rocket equation, sunlight and signal delay, and three difficulty levels for different student levels.
One to four players can team up as Mission Director, Engineer, Science Lead or Comms & Operations Lead. Each controls their own subsystems, and the crew must approve the design before launch.
We built it around NASA's resources: the four mission segments, Mission Design Lab disciplines, Concept Maturity Levels, CubeSat 101, Mission Viz, and comparisons with real missions such as Landsat 9.
Students learn why designs succeed or fail by safely trying them.
details:
SKY RIFT

Design it. Launch it. Learn why it worked, or why it didn't.

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Project summary for submission

Team: SkyRift · Challenge: Space Mission Design Game

Live game:https://skyrift-wheat.vercel.app/ · Code: https://github.com/Mr-Sherin/SkyRift

Overview

SKY RIFT is a browser-based game that teaches the trade-offs of real space mission design. Players take the role of a mission team at a small space agency. They choose a mission, build a spacecraft from realistic subsystems, pick a launch vehicle, pass a preflight check, and then fly the mission turn by turn, making decisions under pressure. Every choice has a visible consequence. There is no single perfect solution, only trade-offs between mass, power, fuel, budget, data, and communications.

The challenge we chose

Space engineering is usually taught as formulas on a page. Students rarely see how the rocket equation, solar power, battery capacity, and data downlink interact in one design. We chose the Space Mission Design Game challenge because we wanted students to feel those trade-offs: add one more instrument and the craft gets heavier, so it needs more fuel and more power, and that raises the cost.

How the game works

1.       Choose a mission. Four missions of increasing difficulty: Orbital Sentinel (Earth observation from low Earth orbit), Artemis Surveyor (lunar polar water-ice mapping), Red Frontier (Mars orbit), and Deep Primitive (asteroid Bennu). Missions unlock in sequence.

2.       Build in the Hangar. Players install parts across eight categories (frame, power, engine, communications, navigation, thermal, computing, science) in a 3D hangar. A live resource panel tracks budget, weight, Δv, and power balance.

3.       Choose a launch vehicle. Each rocket shows its lift capacity, margin, launch cost, reliability, and its impact on the remaining budget.

4.       Pass Preflight Diagnostics. The game explains each blocker in plain language (for example, "Δv short by 233 m/s") and shows how to fix it. In harder modes, players can launch anyway and accept the risk.

5.       Launch and fly. After a countdown and stage separation, the mission runs for eight turns. Each turn the player chooses to observe, downlink data, conserve power, or perform a maneuver, while a trajectory view and live meters (battery, data, propellant, health) show the result.

6.       Respond to anomalies. Random events such as micrometeoroid hits, ground-station dropouts, solar storms, and battery over-temperature warnings require decisions, each with trade-offs.

7.       Debrief. A score breakdown, a segment scorecard, root-cause explanations, and suggested next steps tell the player why the mission succeeded or failed, so each attempt becomes a lesson.

What makes it educational

•         Consequences are explicit. Failing a mission teaches something. The debrief names the cause and suggests a change.

•         Learning is in context. Short hints appear at the moment they matter, such as a Δv blocker or an anomaly. Each anomaly includes a "What real missions do" note connecting the decision to real spacecraft practice.

•         Three difficulty levels. Beginner mode simplifies the catalog, adds forgiving margins, and uses plain-language tips. Standard and Expert add tighter budgets and more frequent anomalies.

•         A Learn page explains the three core rules behind the game (the rocket equation, sunlight falling off with distance, and signal delay) with worked values and links to NASA tools.

Team play

The game supports one to four players. In team mode, each player takes a role (Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, or Communications & Operations Lead) and can modify only their own subsystems. Each role has a private goal, such as keeping mass low or maximizing science return. Before ignition, the crew must sign off on the design in a design review, or reject it with a reason. Empty roles can be filled by the room host, so a game is never blocked by missing teammates.

How we used NASA and space agency resources

We built SKY RIFT around the resources provided for this challenge:

•         NASA's four mission segments (launch, space, ground, and user) structure our flow and our debrief scorecard.

•         Mission Design Lab disciplines informed the eight Hangar categories.

•         Concept Maturity Levels shaped our difficulty tiers (idea and feasibility, trade study, point design) and the crew design review.

•         The Webb "Build It Yourself" satellite game inspired the link between mission objective, instrument choice, and similar real missions.

•         CubeSat 101 grounded the small-satellite beginner mission.

•         NASA Mission Viz is linked on the Learn page for further exploration.

•         Our debrief compares each design with real missions such as Landsat 9, and a NASA Sources & Credits page lists the references we used. Values we simplified are marked as such. [Add if completed: validation tests that compare our calculations with independent reference calculations.]

Story and engagement

To make the engineering memorable, the game follows a crew at a small space agency: a flight director, an engineer, a science lead, a communications officer, and a funding board chair. Their trust in the player changes with the player's decisions. A daily challenge, achievements, and a campaign across four missions encourage replay.

Accessibility and reach

SKY RIFT runs in a web browser with no installation, and is designed for students at different levels through its difficulty modes. [Add only what you finish: mobile layout, keyboard navigation, colorblind-safe indicators, a second language for the Beginner path.]

Impact

Our goal is that students leave understanding why a spacecraft design succeeds or fails, not just a vocabulary list. [Add if you run it: "We tested the game with N students. On a 3-question concept check, scores rose from X to Y on average, and N of N said they would play again."]

Technology and use of AI

SKY RIFT is a web application built with Next.js and React, with a 3D hangar scene, a turn-based mission simulation, and real-time room synchronization for team play. We used AI coding assistants (including Google Antigravity and Claude) to speed up development and to review our design. Our team set the game design, learning goals, rules, and content; tested and corrected the results; and takes responsibility for the final product. [State what existed before the event and what you built during it, according to the 2026 rules.]

Looking ahead

With more time, we would load live NASA mission data into the part and mission catalogs, add more destinations and mission types, publish a teacher guide and classroom mode, add more languages, and let teams compete on shared challenges.
